title: Animator Clister Santos makes peace with his absent mother in 3D short
summary: In ‘Sana’y Nandito Ka,’ Clister Santos turns his longing for his mother into an animated short film that confronts the unfinished business of their separate lives

blocks.text: When he was in senior high school, 25-year-old animator and filmmaker Clister Santos’ mother moved from Marikina to Bicol to live a life she had always wanted. Living with his grandmother since then has made him yearn for a maternal figure, affecting their relationship and making it more distant.

Now that he is producing films, Clister wrote, directed, and produced a 3D animated short film inspired by his relationship with his mother, told through the lens of a child acknowledging her decisions.

His 21-minute animated film Sana’y Nandito Ka follows 24-year-old Kyle as he reunites with his mother, Loren, after six years of separation, thanks to an election in their city. As they spend the day together, they confront the awkwardness, unspoken emotions, and lingering love. Their brief meeting makes Kyle recognize his feelings about his mother’s absence and feel a strange sense of familiarity as she leaves him again.

This material, however, was originally planned for production in 2024, as he first pitched it to the QCinema International Film Festival under the QCShorts production grant or short film category, hosted by Quezon City — a UNESCO Creative City of Film — but it was only shortlisted.
Fast forward to 2026: Clister got invited to present it again to the film festival for possible funding and selection.
“Tapos sabi ko, parang ayoko nang ituloy kasi parang ayoko na. Parang tapos na yung kuwento na ganyan-ganyan. Hindi ko na siya i-pursue,” Clister shared.
(I told myself I would discontinue it because I’m not interested anymore — the story has been written. I no longer want to pursue it.)

blocks.caption: BUS RIDE. A still from the film ‘Sana’y Nandito Ka.’ Photo courtesy of On’tus Films and Chanoma Studios

blocks.text: The same week of their pitching, his mother invited him to Bicol for Holy Week. There, he visited their town for the first time in six years, which led him to realize the film should approach a mother’s story with empathy rather than anger.
“Pagka-uwi, sabi ko, sige, i-rewrite ko yung buong screenplay. Tapos nag-iba na yung angulo ko sa kuwento,” Clister said.
(When I got home, I told myself I would rewrite the screenplay, then I changed the angle of my story.)
Lo and behold, he was selected as one of five finalists out of 395 submissions from Filipino filmmakers globally in the same category at the film festival, receiving a P700,000 production grant.

Currently working at an advertising agency, Clister is no stranger to animation, having earned a multimedia arts degree with a concentration in animation at CIIT College of Arts and Technology in 2024.

His thesis film Ili-Ili (Little One) even won first place in the animation category of the CCP Gawad Alternatibo and was selected as a finalist at the BFI Flare: London LGBTQIA+ Film Festival in the year of his graduation.
He has also been one of the animators on full-length animated films in the country, such as Avid Liongoren’s Zsazsa Zaturnnah vs. the Amazonistas of Planet X and Carl Papa’s 58th and Patay Gutom.
His decision to pursue an animation program wasn’t easy, though, as he originally planned to study architecture or civil engineering, his parents’ preferred paths.
Thankfully, he competed in the 2018 National Digital Arts Awards (NDAA) in the animation contest under the student category, getting the second-place award in high school.
Little did he know, first-place winners were given scholarships to pursue a college degree program of their choice.

“Since yung nanalo ng first place nung batch namin, college na sila, sa akin nila binigay yung scholarship kasi magte-take pa lang ako ng college. Tapos, in a way, na-take ko pa rin yung animation,” Clister narrated.
(Since the first-place winners in our batch were already college students, they gave me the scholarship because I was about to enter college. In a way, I was able to take animation.)

blocks.caption: WINNER. Clister (middle) receives the Special Prize award of NDAA 2018, receiving a full scholarship at CIIT College of Arts and Technology in 2019. Photo courtesy of CIIT College of Arts and Technology

blocks.text: When he finished his degree two years ago, his mother couldn’t attend his graduation. Clister understood his mother’s absence. For him, it wasn’t because she didn’t care, but because she was already living out her dream of a happy life.
“After years of watching her unhappy, I couldn’t be angry about that. I still can’t,” his director’s statement reads.
The young animator-filmmaker told Rappler that working on the film made him understand his mother’s decisions — why she left him and why she did it — six years ago.
His personal narrative pushed him to tell a familiar story through an animated short film, as it is what he knows best as a storyteller.
Clister shared that he pursued this treatment because most animated films in the country are only for children or fantastical, featuring characters with powers, monsters, or aliens.
His treatment of the story was even questioned by some jurors because they thought the script was intended for live action.
“Ito yung gusto kong i-try ma-push, kahit papaano, na ma-introduce sa Philippines na puwede pala yung mga ganitong kuwento sa animation,” he told Rappler.
(I want to introduce that these kinds of stories can also be told in animated films in the Philippines.)

“It’s just na hindi lang dapat nalilimitahan yung puwedeng ikuwento sa animation. Kasi parang never pa ako nakakita ng 3D animation na parang slice of life lang, parang makikita [mo lang siya] sa live action,” he added.
(We must not limit the stories told in animation. I think I haven’t seen a 3D animation that features a slice of life; it is only done in live action.)

blocks.caption: BEHIND THE SCENE. Zaijian Jaranilla and Meryll Soriano perform in front of two cameras as the production team captures a scene for ‘Sana’y Nandito Ka.’ Photo by Roaze Alcaide

blocks.text: His approach to animation follows, however, the practices of other animation productions in the country: performance-first. This style requires actors to act first in front of a camera, which serves as a reference for the animation.
The young filmmaker chose 3D animation deliberately because it is rare in independent filmmaking in the Philippines, with most pursuing 2D.

The first 3D animated entry in the QCShorts stars Zaijian Jaranilla — who last starred in the 3D animated film RPG Metanoia almost 16 years ago — as the son, and Meryll Soriano as the mother. The cast also includes Harvey Bautista and Jeula Agbayani.

Clister worked on the animation alone in his previous films. For Sana’y Nandito Ka, however, he teamed up with over 20 animators — mostly students — and together they completed every shot of the film in three months.
When asked why he changed his approach this time, he said it was for convenience because film and voice actors usually record voices for animated films.

“Tapos, i-acting namin yun, ibi-video namin yung sarili namin, parang dina-dub namin yung [boses] nila. Tapos ang nangyayari, inconsistent siya sa emosyon ng iba’t ibang shots. So hindi siya nagtutugma every time,” Clister said.

(We will take a video of ourselves acting it, dubbing their voices, which serves as a reference for our animation. And then what happens is, it’s inconsistent with the emotions of the different shots. So it doesn’t match up every time.)

Through this treatment, the young animator expressed surprise at observing specific performance choices by the actors on set. He analyzed their acting intent, examining subtle details such as eye blinks and gaze directions.

blocks.caption: TEAM WORK. Young Filipino animators collaboratively animate their scenes for the film. Photo by Roaze Alcaide

blocks.text: “TV actors, film actors, alam nila yung camera, ganyan. May mga intention sila sa pag-act nila. Dinala ko sa animation na mas guide siya sa mga animators,” Clister added.
(They are television and film actors, so they know how to act in front of the camera. They have their own intentions when they act. I brought it into animation so animators had a guide.)
As the short film runs at QCinema until November 22 across select Quezon City cinemas, Clister hopes audiences will appreciate the true intention of the story.
“Sana mayroon ding part na makita nila sa sarili nila kay Kyle or even kay Loren, yung mama sa [kuwento], yung nais [na iparating ng] film,” Clister noted.
(I hope they also see a part of themselves in Kyle or even in Loren, the mother in the film, which we wanted to convey in the film.)

blocks.caption: CAST. Animator Clister Santos (center) poses with actors (from left) Zaijian Jaranilla, Jeula Agbayani, Harvey Bautista, and Meryll Soriano after wrapping up their shoot in August 2026. Photo by Roaze Alcaide

blocks.text: Clister shares that part of being an adult is to sometimes seek a parental figure. “[But] just have to live [a] life na di sana tayo nababurden lagi na na-held back tayo ng mga what-ifs natin sa buhay,” he added.
(But you just have to live a life where we do not feel burdened or held back by our what-ifs.)
With the short film’s title translated as “I Wish You Were Here” in English, Clister wants to highlight a story of two people trying to be seen and taking a leap of faith to start over.

“I’m not making this film to resolve anything,” Clister writes in his director’s statement. “I’m making this because I think there are lots of us who want to hug our mothers back a little too late.” – Rappler.com
